content.overview: Article 31 (Compulsory acquisition of property) was omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, section 6, with effect from 20 June 1979. The right to property is no longer a Fundamental Right. The living protection is Article 300A: no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.
content.glance: Art 31 omitted by 44th Amendment (1978, w.e.f. 20-6-1979). Property is now a constitutional legal right under Article 300A, not a Fundamental Right under Part III.
content.study:
Article 31 originally guaranteed that no person would be deprived of property save by authority of law and regulated compulsory acquisition for public purposes with compensation. It was part of Part III (Fundamental Rights).

Omission: Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 6 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979). The same amendment inserted Article 300A in Part XII, Chapter IV, converting the protection into a constitutional legal right (not enforceable as a Fundamental Right under Article 32).

Articles 31A, 31B and 31C were not omitted and continue to save certain acquisition, agrarian-reform and Directive-Principle laws from specified Fundamental Rights challenges.

Examination rule: Do not cite Article 31 as living law. For contemporary property deprivation, cite Article 300A and the governing statute (e.g. land acquisition law). For historical questions, state the 44th Amendment omission and the shift from Fundamental Right to legal right.

sections.heading: Constitutional status and amendment
sections.body:
Article 31 is omitted. The authoritative notation in the official text is that it was omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 6 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979). It forms no part of the living enforceable Part III text.

Purpose of omission: to reduce litigation against land-reform and public-purpose acquisition measures that had repeatedly been challenged when property was a Fundamental Right, while retaining a basic legality requirement under Article 300A.

sections.heading: Successor provision — Article 300A
sections.body:
Article 300A provides: ‘No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.’

Consequences:
1. Property is a constitutional legal right, not a Fundamental Right.
2. Deprivation requires authority of law (no pure executive deprivation).
3. Article 32 is not available solely for a pure Article 300A claim; remedy is ordinarily under Article 226 or ordinary civil process, subject to the applicable statute.
4. Adequacy of compensation and public purpose are governed primarily by the acquisition statute and judicial review standards developed under Article 300A and related doctrine, not by the omitted Article 31 text.

sections.heading: Articles 31A, 31B and 31C (still in force)
sections.body:
The omission of Article 31 did not repeal the ‘Saving of Certain Laws’ provisions:
- Article 31A — saving of laws providing for acquisition of estates etc.
- Article 31B — validation of Acts and Regulations in the Ninth Schedule (subject to basic-structure review after I.R. Coelho).
- Article 31C — saving of laws giving effect to certain Directive Principles (Article 39(b) and (c) core; broader 42nd Amendment expansion later limited by judicial review).

These remain relevant to land reform, nationalisation and socio-economic legislation challenges.

sections.heading: Exam and drafting checkpoints
sections.body:
1. State clearly that Article 31 is omitted (44th Amendment, 1978).
2. Identify Article 300A as the living constitutional protection for property.
3. Do not treat property deprivation as a Part III Fundamental Rights claim under Article 32 unless another living Fundamental Right (e.g. Article 14 or 21) is also engaged.
4. Distinguish omitted Article 31 from living Articles 31A–31C.
5. For problem questions on acquisition, apply the current statute plus Article 300A legality, not the repealed compensation clauses of old Article 31.

examples.title: Illustration — Post-1979 acquisition challenge
examples.body: A landowner challenges a 2020 statutory acquisition solely under ‘Article 31’. The challenge is misconceived: Article 31 stands omitted. The proper constitutional frame is Article 300A (authority of law) together with the acquisition statute and, where pleaded, Articles 14 and 21.

examples.title: Illustration — Continuing role of Article 31A
examples.body: A state agrarian-reform law is attacked as violating Articles 14 and 19. Article 31A may still be invoked (where its conditions are met) to save specified estate-acquisition laws from those challenges, even though Article 31 itself is omitted.

hypotheticals.question: Can a petitioner in 2026 enforce a pure Article 31 claim for inadequate compensation?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Article 31 was omitted by the 44th Amendment with effect from 20 June 1979. The living constitutional provision is Article 300A. Compensation and procedure are governed by the applicable acquisition statute and judicial review under Article 300A / Article 14 / Article 21 as pleaded. Reformulate the petition accordingly.

rows.left: Was a Fundamental Right in Part III
rows.right: Legal right in Part XII; not a Fundamental Right
Primarily Article 226 / ordinary process; not pure Article 32 on 300A alone

misconceptions.trap: Article 31 is still the source of the right to property.
misconceptions.correction: Article 31 is omitted. The living constitutional source is Article 300A.

misconceptions.trap: Articles 31A–31C were also repealed with Article 31.
misconceptions.correction: Articles 31A, 31B and 31C remain in force and continue to save certain laws from specified Fundamental Rights challenges.

misconceptions.trap: After omission of Article 31, the State may take property without any law.
misconceptions.correction: Article 300A still requires authority of law. Pure executive deprivation without statutory authority is unconstitutional.

questionsAndAnswers.question: State the present constitutional status of Article 31 and identify the living provision that protects property.
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Article 31 (Compulsory acquisition of property) was omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, section 6, with effect from 20 June 1979. It is not living law. The living constitutional protection is Article 300A: no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law. Property is a constitutional legal right, not a Fundamental Right. Articles 31A–31C remain in force for specified saving purposes.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: Accurate status + successor + surviving companion articles.

Redirect contemporary property claims to Article 300A and the governing statute.
Do not conflate omitted Article 31 with living Articles 31A–31C.

learningObjectives: State that Article 31 was omitted by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979).
Identify Article 300A as the living constitutional protection for property.
Distinguish omitted Article 31 from living Articles 31A–31C.
Apply the correct remedial frame (Article 300A + statute, not omitted Article 31) in problem questions.
enhancement.definition: Article 31 was the original Part III guarantee concerning compulsory acquisition of property. It was omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978. The living protection is Article 300A.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Omission of a Fundamental Right by constitutional amendment removes it from Part III; a substituted constitutional legal right (Article 300A) may continue to require authority of law for deprivation of property.
keyTakeaways: Do not cite Article 31 as current law in 2026 disputes.
